summary: A draft table of contents for a planned Internet Protocol Handbook, a collection of the main internet-family RFCs and experiment notes. It was meant to replace the old ARPANET protocol documents as the internet protocols took over. Replaced by RFC 774.

eli5.summary: Imagine a librarian making a list of chapters for a big binder of rules. This memo is that list, and people were asked to suggest chapters to add.

questions: internet protocol handbook table of contents
what was the internet protocol handbook
how were early internet protocols documented
what protocols went into the handbook
subtitle: Draft outline for a handbook of internet protocols

tldr.problem: Internet protocols were scattered across experiment notes and RFCs with no unified reference guide as they replaced older ARPANET protocols.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 766 proposes a table of contents for an Internet Protocol Handbook that would collect the main internet protocol RFCs in one place, organized by layer: gateway, host, and application level.
tldr.outcome: This draft led to RFC 774, which superseded it with a revised handbook plan.

today: RFC 766 is a historic meta-RFC that was superseded by RFC 774. It documents the planning of early protocol documentation efforts.

sections.title: Background
sections.content: As the ARPA Network Research Program's work on interconnecting networks matured, a family of internet protocols emerged from research documented in Internet Experiment Notes (IENs) and RFCs. By 1980, the internet protocol family had grown mature enough to replace the old ARPANET protocols. RFC 766 announces that an Internet Protocol Handbook will be compiled by the Network Information Center to serve as the authoritative reference for this new protocol family, paralleling the old ARPANET Protocol Handbook.
sections.eli5: The internet protocols were documented in scattered memos. This memo says there will be a handbook collecting them all in one organized place.

sections.title: Proposed Contents
sections.content:
The draft handbook organizes protocols by layer. Gateway Level covers the Internet Datagram Protocol (IP), gateway building, and gateway monitoring. Host Level includes User Datagram Protocol (UDP), Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), and multiplexing. Application Level encompasses time, name, and file transfer services, Telnet, and mail protocols. Appendices cover assigned numbers, protocol options, address mappings, and mail standards.

Most of these protocols already existed as either IENs or RFCs. The handbook was to be a compilation and organization of existing documents rather than new specifications.
sections.eli5: The handbook would sort protocols into layers: how to send data, how to manage connections, and what applications can do. Most were already written; they just needed to be collected.

sections.title: Accessing the Documents
sections.content: At the time of RFC 766, RFCs and IENs were available for download from the Network Information Center at SRI-KL via FTP. IENs had pathnames like <NETINFO>IEN-nnn.TXT while RFCs used <NETINFO>RFCnnn.TXT (note the different hyphenation). The RFC notes that this naming inconsistency made it easy to confuse the two document types.
sections.eli5: You could get the documents from a computer at Stanford using FTP, using special folder names to find IENs or RFCs.
